title: Renewable Energy & Electric Mobility
tagline: Safety first, then deployable, then optimal — clean energy and the vehicles it drives, built for Indian conditions.

intro.text: Every derating factor in this chapter is a number that a textbook treats as a footnote and an Indian installation treats as the main event. Together they are the difference between a system that meets its generation estimate and one that quietly under-performs for a decade.

blocks.text: A module rated 550 W is rated at Standard Test Conditions: 1000 W/m², cell temperature 25 °C, AM1.5 spectrum. Those conditions occur on an Indian rooftop almost never. What you actually get is the nameplate multiplied by a chain of losses:
Loss Typical India Cause and what you do about it

Temperature 8–16% Module power falls roughly 0.3–0.4% per °C above 25 °C. At 42 °C ambient a roof-mounted cell can sit near 65 °C — that is 40 °C above STC, so 12–16% gone before anything else. Mitigate: 100 mm+ clearance under the module for airflow, never flush-mount on a hot roof

Soiling 3–25% Dust, bird droppings, pollen, construction dust, cement plant fallout. In Rajasthan, Delhi-NCR and Gujarat, uncleaned arrays can lose well over 20% by the end of the dry season. Mitigate: a cleaning schedule (§2.6), and tilt ≥ 10° so rain sheds rather than pools

Mismatch and  2–8%                            Modules in a string perform to the weakest. A single shaded module drags the string. Mitigate: shading
shading                                       survey (§2.2), string layout by shade group, module-level electronics only where a real obstruction
                                              exists
DC and AC wiring 2–4%                         I²R losses. Long DC runs on undersized cable are the usual culprit. Mitigate: size cable for ≤ 2% drop
                                              (§2.5), not merely for ampacity
Inverter      2–5%                            Conversion efficiency, plus poor performance when loaded far below rating. Mitigate: size the inverter
                                              to the array, typically 1.1–1.3 DC:AC ratio
Availability  1–5%                            Grid outages (a grid-tied inverter must shut down when the grid fails), faults, maintenance. Mitigate:
                                              this is where hybrid or off-grid architectures earn their cost
Multiply them out and a well-built Indian rooftop system runs at a Performance Ratio of about 0.75–0.82. Use 0.78 for a first estimate and measure your own after six months.

topics.title: Monsoon and dust are one design problem, not two

blocks.text: The seasonal cycle you are designing against

Dry season (roughly Feb–June). Soiling accumulates steadily — in dusty regions the loss climbs by a percent or two every month with no rain to clear it. Generation is high but the array is getting progressively dirtier, and this is when cleaning pays for itself.

Monsoon (June–Sept). Generation drops sharply on overcast days — plan for the worst month, not the average. But rain also cleans the array for free, so soiling loss falls to near zero. The design risks shift to water ingress, corrosion, and lightning.

Post-monsoon (Oct–Jan). Usually the best generation of the year: clean modules, clear skies, cooler cells. If your system does not perform in November, something is wrong that has nothing to do with the weather.

• Design the water path, do not just seal. Junction boxes face downward, cable glands enter from below, and every enclosure has a drip loop before it and a drainage point at its lowest corner. Water always gets in eventually; what matters is whether it can get out.
• Use the right ingress protection and mean it. IP65 minimum for outdoor enclosures, IP67 where standing water is possible. An IP65 box with an unsealed cable entry is an IP20 box.

• Earthing and lightning are not optional in India. Module frames and mounting structure bonded to a dedicated earth; a surge protection device on both the DC and AC side. A single nearby strike will take out an unprotected inverter, and it is the most common insurance claim in Indian rooftop solar.
• Tilt for rain, not only for yield. A near-flat array traps dust and pooled water. Even where the optimum tilt is low, keep at least 10–15° so the monsoon does your cleaning.
• Corrosion. Coastal and high-humidity sites need stainless or hot-dip galvanised hardware. Ordinary zinc-plated bolts will be rust stains within two monsoons.

topics.title: Grid instability and what it does to your design

topics.title: Affordability decides whether it gets built

blocks.text: A technically superior system that nobody can finance does not reduce any emissions. Learn to speak in the two numbers that decision-makers actually use — payback period and levelised cost of energy — and to state your assumptions alongside them.
payback (years) = (capital cost - subsidy) / annual savings
3 kW rooftop, roughly Rs 1,90,000 installed, PM Surya Ghar subsidy Rs 78,000
Generation = 3 kWp x 5.0 PSH x 0.78 PR x 365 = 4,270 kWh/year
Savings at a tariff of Rs 8/kWh = Rs 34,160/year
Without the subsidy it is 5.6 years. That gap IS the policy working.
LEVELISED COST OF ENERGY - the number that lets you compare technologies LCOE = (lifetime cost) / (lifetime energy delivered)
Lifetime cost = capital - subsidy + O&M over 25 yr
Lifetime energy = 4,270 kWh/yr, degrading ~0.5%/yr over 25 yr
Compare that against a grid tariff of Rs 8/kWh and the case makes itself. Compare it against a diesel genset at Rs 20-25/kWh and it is not close.

Every number above depends on: peak sun hours at YOUR site, the tariff YOU pay (slab tariffs mean the marginal unit may cost far more than the average), whether you get the subsidy, and a discount rate if you are being rigorous. Quote a range, not a single figure.
Run this before you design anything. If the payback exceeds the customer’s planning horizon, the correct engineering response is to change the design, not to argue with them

DO THIS NOW — Build your own derating stack An hour. Do this for a real roof you can stand on. 1 Find the peak sun hours for your district (§2.1). Write down the source and the month-by-month figures, not just the
annual average. 2 Estimate each loss in §1.1 for that specific site. Justify each in one line — ‘soiling 12% because the site is 400 m from a

cement road and cleaning will realistically be quarterly’. 3 Multiply them out to get your own Performance Ratio. Compare it against 0.78. 4 Compute expected annual generation for a 3 kWp system and the simple payback at your local tariff. 5 Now redo the payback for the worst monsoon month rather than the annual average, and note how differently the system
looks. Designing to the average is how off-grid systems end up undersized.

intro.text: Most failed installations were decided at the assessment stage. By the time anyone is on the roof with a drill, the important decisions have already been made — and the expensive mistakes are the ones made before the first component was ordered.

Convert irradiance to peak sun hours (PSH): the daily GHI in kWh/m² is numerically the number of hours of 1000 W/m² equivalent. Most of India sits between 4.5 and 6.0 PSH annually — Rajasthan and Gujarat at the top, the north-east and Kerala lower. Use the worst month for off-grid sizing and the annual average for grid-tied. That single choice is the most common sizing error in student projects.

Step 3 is where lead-acid quietly loses. Halving the depth of discharge doubles the pack you must buy, and the cycle life difference then compounds on top of that.

topics.title: String sizing — the calculation that protects the inverter

blocks.text: Modules in series must satisfy TWO limits at the same time, computed at OPPOSITE temperature extremes. Getting this wrong destroys inverters.

MODULE      Voc 49.5 V · Vmp 41.2 V
            Voc temp coefficient -0.27 %/C
INVERTER    Vmp temp coefficient -0.35 %/C
SITE        max DC input 1000 V · MPPT window 200 - 850 V
            lowest expected cell temp 0 C · highest cell temp 70 C
UPPER LIMIT - set by the COLDEST morning, because Voc RISES as it cools
max modules in series = 1000 / 52.84 = 18.9 -> 18 modules

This is the one people get wrong. They size at 25 C, get 20 modules, and the string exceeds 1000 V on the first cold clear morning in January - before the inverter has even started, at open circuit, when nothing is drawing current and Voc is at its absolute maximum.
LOWER LIMIT - set by the HOTTEST afternoon, because Vmp FALLS as it heats
min modules in series = 200 / 34.71 = 5.8 -> 6 modules
Below this the string drops out of the MPPT window on hot afternoons and the inverter simply stops tracking - you lose the generation with no fault indication at all.
RESULT: 6 to 18 modules per string. Design at 16 - 17 for headroom, not at 18. Module Voc tolerance and future colder-than-expected mornings both eat the margin.
ALWAYS use YOUR site's record low temperature, not the seasonal average, and YOUR module's datasheet coefficients, not the values above.

Sourcing routes: national distributors and OEM dealers for modules and inverters; local electrical wholesale markets for cable, protection and hardware; online marketplaces for small components and dev boards. Prices move with module and cell markets — always re-quote.

• Size cable for voltage drop, not just current. Target ≤ 2% on the DC side and ≤ 1% on the AC side. A cable that is thermally adequate can still waste several percent of your generation for twenty-five years.

• Torque every electrical connection to specification and mark it. Loose DC connections heat, oxidise, and are the leading cause of rooftop solar fires. A paint pen witness mark makes a loosened joint visible at a glance during maintenance.
• Crimp MC4 connectors with the correct tool and pull-test every one. A hand-squeezed MC4 is a future arc.
• Earth the frames, the structure and the inverter to a dedicated earth pit; measure the earth resistance and record it.

• Label everything — strings, polarity, isolators, and a clear placard at the main panel saying that the building has a solar installation with a second source of supply. A fire crew needs to know that before they cut anything.
• Leave a maintenance path. If cleaning requires walking on modules, the array will not be cleaned.

Measure the Performance Ratio, not just the kWh. PR is actual generation divided by what the measured irradiance should have produced. It normalises for weather, which raw kWh does not — a system generating less in July is not necessarily faulty, but a system whose PR has fallen from 0.80 to 0.68 definitely is.
Task Frequency What it catches

against expectation
Compute Performance Ratio Monthly Gradual degradation that raw kWh hides
Visual inspection: cracks, Quarterly Most physical failures before they become electrical ones discolouration, water in junction boxes, rodent damage
Clean the modules Site-dependent: The largest recoverable loss on most Indian sites monthly in dusty regions, quarterly elsewhere; not needed during monsoon
Check and re-torque connections; Annually Loose and hot joints before they arc thermal-scan with an IR camera under load

String-level I–V curve or per-string Annually                        A weak or failing module hiding inside a healthy-looking array
current comparison
Clean early in the morning with plain water and a soft brush. Never spray cold water on hot glass — thermal shock cracks modules — and never clean an array standing on it.

DO THIS NOW — Size a real system end to end Three hours. Use an actual building you have access to. 1 Collect twelve months of electricity bills and extract monthly kWh. This is your load, and it is far better than any appliance

estimate. 2 Do the site survey checklist properly, including the winter shading assessment. 3 Fill in the sizing worksheet in §2.3 for both grid-tied and off-grid. Note the ratio between the two array sizes. 4 Price it from the sourcing table, then check every module you have chosen against the ALMM list. 5 Compute payback and LCOE from §1.4 both with and without the PM Surya Ghar subsidy. 6 Write one paragraph recommending an architecture — grid-tied, hybrid or off-grid — and defend it using the outage
frequency at that specific site, not a general preference.

intro.text: Everyone arrives with instincts trained on mains AC. Almost all of them are wrong for photovoltaic strings and battery packs. This chapter is short, and it is the one chapter in this guide that is not negotiable.

topics.title: Why DC is more dangerous than the voltage suggests

blocks.text: • A DC arc does not go out on its own. Alternating current crosses zero a hundred times a second, and an arc extinguishes at each crossing — this is what lets an ordinary switch break an AC circuit. DC has no zero crossing. Once struck, a DC arc sustains itself and will happily burn until something melts. This is why every isolator, breaker and fuse in a DC circuit must be DC-rated at or above the system voltage. An AC-rated device in a DC circuit may weld shut or burn rather than interrupt.

• A photovoltaic array cannot be switched off. If there is light on it, it is generating. You can open the circuit downstream, but the module terminals and the cable up to your isolator remain live. Covering an array with an opaque sheet reduces but does not reliably eliminate output. Treat every PV conductor as live at all times during daylight.

• A battery cannot be switched off either. It has no off state. A pack is a very low impedance source that will deliver hundreds of amps into a short without any warning noise, and the result is molten metal rather than a tripped breaker.

• Current, not voltage, injures you. The often-quoted figure is that currents in the low tens of milliamps through the chest can be fatal. Whether that happens depends on skin resistance, path and duration — which is why wet hands, a cut, or a path from one hand to the other are what turn a survivable contact into a lethal one.
The voltage thresholds you need to know

Below about 60 V DC is generally treated as extra-low voltage and is the band in which supervised student work is reasonable. It is not ‘safe’ — a 48 V pack will still deliver an arc that destroys a spanner and your eyesight — but the electrocution risk is much reduced.

60 V DC and above is treated as hazardous live in vehicle standards, and IEC practice treats 120 V DC as the ripple-free extra-low-voltage limit in dry conditions. A typical solar string runs 300–600 V DC and an EV traction pack 350–800 V DC. Both are lethal and both are outside the scope of unsupervised student work.

The projects in this guide are scoped to stay below 60 V DC precisely so that they can be built in a college lab. Where a real installation exceeds that — the charging station in Chapter 4 — the guide tells you which parts must be done by a licensed contractor.

topics.title: Lithium batteries: the failure mode to respect

blocks.text: A lithium cell that is over-charged, over-discharged, punctured, crushed, overheated or internally short-circuited can enter thermal runaway: an exothermic reaction that heats the cell, which accelerates the reaction, which heats it further. Once started it cannot be stopped by removing the electrical fault, and it can propagate cell to cell through a pack.

• It vents toxic gas. Electrolyte decomposition products include hydrogen fluoride. A pack venting in an enclosed room is a serious inhalation hazard independent of the fire risk. Never charge or test packs in an unventilated space.
• It can reignite. Hours later. A pack that has been in thermal runaway is not safe because the flames stopped; it needs prolonged cooling and isolated storage.

• Do not fight a pack fire as a student. Evacuate, raise the alarm, call the fire service and tell them it is a lithium battery. For a genuinely small incipient event, copious water is the correct cooling agent for lithium-ion (this is the opposite of the rule for lithium metal primary cells, which is where the ‘never water’ folklore comes from). The realistic student control is prevention plus containment, not extinguishing.

• Containment is cheap. Charge and test packs inside a metal box or on a non-combustible surface, away from anything that burns, with a bucket of dry sand and a fire blanket within reach and a clear path to the door.
• Second-life cells carry unknown history. A pack pulled from a crashed or flood-damaged vehicle may have mechanical or internal damage you cannot see. Chapter 6 sets specific rules for this.

TEST - VERIFY - TEST (the only correct way to confirm something is dead) 1. Test your meter on a known live source. It works. 2. Test the conductor you believe is dead. It reads zero. 3. Test your meter on the known live source AGAIN. It still works. Only now is the conductor proven dead. Step 3 catches the blown fuse or flat battery in your meter, which is exactly how people are killed by circuits they "checked".

Work with one hand; keep the other in your pocket or behind your back. A hand-to-hand path crosses the heart. A hand-to-same-side path may not. Stand on a dry insulating mat. Never lean on the chassis or the rack.

Open the isolator, lock it open, and hang a tag with YOUR name and the date. One person controls one lock. Never rely on a switch someone else could close while you have your hands inside the enclosure.

Remove watch, rings, chain, metal bracelet. A ring across a pack terminal becomes a heating element welded to your finger. Use insulated tools. Tape over the exposed metal of any spanner you must bring near terminals. Never place a tool on top of a battery.

Always: safety glasses, closed shoes, cotton or FR clothing (not synthetic - it melts onto skin) Battery work: nitrile gloves under insulating gloves, face shield when making or breaking a high-current connection Rooftop: harness and anchor above about 2 m, and NEVER on a wet roof
Never work alone on any energised system. The second person is not there to help; they are there to disconnect power and call for help.
Photograph every connection before you disconnect it. On a battery or an array you will not remember the polarity an hour later, and reversed polarity destroys equipment and starts fires
CHECKLIST — Hard limits for student work — these are limits, not guidance

□ Nothing above 60 V DC without a qualified supervisor       □ Sand bucket and fire blanket within arm’s reach
    physically present                                           whenever a pack is on charge

□ No work on any live circuit — isolate, lock out, then □ No metal jewellery, no loose sleeves, insulated tools only test-verify-test □ PV array treated as live in all daylight, always □ Never work alone on an energised system □ Polarity checked twice before every connection is made □ A means of cutting power that can be reached without □ No opening of an EV traction pack, ever, at student level approaching the fault □ No opening or repair of a distribution board or meter — □ Emergency numbers written on the wall, not looked up on licensed electrician only a phone □ Grid connection of any kind is done by a licensed □ Anyone may stop the work at any time, for any reason, contractor, not by you without being questioned □ All DC protection devices DC-rated at or above system voltage
□ Every battery charged and tested in a metal container, ventilated area
DO THIS NOW — Write and rehearse your lab’s emergency procedure
One hour, with everyone who will work on the project present.
1 Walk the room. Identify where power is cut — for the bench, for the room, for the building. Confirm each is reachable without passing the bench.
2 Write, on one page: what to do if a pack starts smoking; what to do if someone is in contact with a live conductor (cut power first, never grab them); who to call; where the nearest hospital is.

3 Put the page on the wall. Put the emergency numbers on it. Do not leave them on a phone. 4 Rehearse the two-minute version out loud with your team. Everyone should be able to say where the isolator is without
looking.
5 Do the test-verify-test procedure on a known circuit until it is automatic. It takes four repetitions to become a habit and it is the habit that matters most.

modules.title: Project 1 — Solar Charging and Battery Swapping for E-Rickshaws

intro.text: An e-rickshaw driver’s constraint is not range. It is the eight hours his vehicle is plugged in and not earning. Battery swapping converts that into a five-minute stop — which is why the design problem is logistics and economics at least as much as it is power electronics.

topics.title: The problem, in the driver’s numbers

blocks.text: FIELD NOTE — Why swapping, not just charging
The economics that decide whether anyone uses your station
THE VEHICLE A typical e-rickshaw carries a 48 V pack of roughly 100 Ah — about 4.8 kWh — giving 80–100 km. Most are still lead-acid, which needs 8–10 hours to charge properly.

THE LOST  Charging at home overnight is fine until demand exceeds one charge. A driver who could earn through a second
DAY       shift cannot, because the vehicle is tethered to a socket.
THE BATTERY A lead-acid pack lasts roughly 12–18 months and costs ₹20,000–₹28,000 to replace. Amortised, that is often the
COST single largest operating cost after the driver’s own time — and it is paid in one painful lump.

WHAT      The driver stops owning the battery. He pays per swap — typically in the ₹80–₹150 range depending on city
SWAPPING  and operator — and drives away in five minutes. Battery degradation, charging discipline and replacement
CHANGES   become the station’s problem, which is exactly where they belong, because the station can charge properly and
          monitor health.

THE CATCH Swapping only works if the packs are physically and electrically standardised. This is the real barrier in India and the reason most swapping networks operate captive fleets rather than open access.

What to take from this: Design the logistics first — how many packs are in circulation, how long each takes to charge, how many slots you need. The solar array is the easy part and the part students always start with.

PV string side (350-600 V DC) and the AC board -> licensed contractor
48 V pack side, slot control, monitoring, UI -> student scope

Figure 4.1 — Note where the boundary sits. Students can design and build the entire 48 V swap cabinet, its control and its monitoring. Nobody unlicensed touches the string wiring or the distribution board.
• One slot, one isolation. Each slot needs its own DC-rated isolator and fuse, so a single faulty pack can be removed without shutting the station.

• Thermal separation between slots. If one pack vents, the design intent is that the failure stops there. Steel dividers, spacing, and vents that direct gas upward and outward rather than into the next slot.
• Forced ventilation, always on when charging. Interlock it: no fan, no charging. Vent to outside air, never into the enclosure or the room.

• Temperature sensing per slot, with charging inhibited above a set limit. Ambient in an Indian summer already sits near the top of the safe charging window for many chemistries, and a charging pack adds its own heat.
• Mechanical keying and a positive latch. A pack must be impossible to insert reversed and impossible to leave half-seated — a partially engaged high-current connector arcs and welds.

• Track every pack. Serial number, cycle count, capacity trend, temperature history. The station’s asset is the fleet of packs, and pack health is your profit and loss. A pack whose capacity has fallen below about 80% goes out of rotation — and becomes the input to Chapter 6.

• Design the queue. Shade, a place to sit, a clear indicator of which slot is ready. Drivers choose stations on convenience, and a station nobody chooses generates no revenue however elegant its power electronics.
// One slot, as a state machine. Runs on the cabinet controller. // Everything here is at 48 V - student scope (ch 3).
typedef enum { EMPTY, INSERTED, VERIFYING, CHARGING, READY, FAULT, LOCKED_OUT } SlotState;
void slotStep(Slot *s, float dt) { switch (s->state) {
case EMPTY: if (s->presenceSwitch && s->latchClosed) s->state = INSERTED; break;
case INSERTED: // never energise on presence alone
s->contactor = OFF;
if (readPackId(s) && packIsKnown(s->packId)) s->state = VERIFYING;
else { s->fault = FAULT_UNKNOWN_PACK; s->state = FAULT; }
break;
case VERIFYING: // check BEFORE closing the contactor
if (s->packVoltage < V_MIN || s->packVoltage > V_MAX) {
s->fault = FAULT_VOLTAGE_RANGE; s->state = FAULT; break;
if (s->packTemp > T_CHARGE_MAX || s->packTemp < T_CHARGE_MIN) {
s->fault = FAULT_TEMPERATURE; s->state = FAULT; break;
if (!ventilationRunning()) break; // interlock: no fan, no charge
s->contactor = ON; s->state = CHARGING; s->t = 0;
break;

case CHARGING: s->t += dt; s->wh += s->volts * s->amps * dt / 3600.0f; if (s->packTemp > T_CHARGE_MAX || !ventilationRunning() || s->amps > I_MAX || s->t > T_TIMEOUT) { s->contactor = OFF; s->fault = FAULT_CHARGING; s->state = FAULT; break; } if (chargeComplete(s)) { s->contactor = OFF; s->state = READY; logCycle(s->packId, s->wh); } break;
case READY:
s->contactor = OFF; // de-energised while waiting
s->readyLamp = ON;
if (!s->presenceSwitch) { s->state = EMPTY; s->readyLamp = OFF; }
break;
case FAULT:
s->contactor = OFF; s->faultLamp = ON;
alertOperator(s->id, s->fault);
if (s->fault == FAULT_TEMPERATURE || s->fault == FAULT_CHARGING)
s->state = LOCKED_OUT; // requires a human, not a timer
break;
case LOCKED_OUT: // only a person with a key clears s->contactor = OFF; // this. A thermal fault must never break; // auto-retry. } }
// 1. The contactor is closed only after verification, never on insertion.
// 2. The slot is de-energised whenever it is not actively charging.
// 3. A thermal fault latches. Auto-retry after a temperature fault is
// how a warm pack becomes a fire.

topics.title: Cost, revenue and the policy hook

blocks.text: Educational institutions can get charging infrastructure funded

Under the PM E-DRIVE charging infrastructure guidelines issued in 2025 for a rollout of around 72,300 public charging points, a tiered subsidy structure applies — and government premises, residential colonies, hospitals and educational institutions are eligible for up to 100% subsidy on upstream infrastructure and charging equipment, provided they guarantee free public access.

For a college project this is directly actionable: a campus station that is publicly accessible may have its charging equipment and upstream electrical work funded. Chapter 7 covers how to check current eligibility, and note that PM E-DRIVE is fund-limited — it closes when the allocation is exhausted, whatever the stated terminal date.
Station cost and revenue model
Line item Basis Capital ₹ Annual ₹ Notes

Capital rows: PV array and canopy · inverter · swap cabinet and chargers · battery fleet (usually the largest) · civil and electrical · load enhancement. Annual rows: grid energy purchased · O&M and cleaning · pack replacement provision · staffing. Revenue: swaps/day × price × 365. Then compute payback both with and without the PM E-DRIVE subsidy — the difference is usually what decides whether the project is viable.

DO THIS NOW — Design the station for your own campus A week. The deliverable is a defensible sizing document, not a render. 1 Count the e-rickshaws that actually operate within two kilometres of your campus. Stand at the gate and count for an hour
at morning and evening peak. That number, not an assumption, is your demand. 2 Interview five drivers: what they pay to charge now, how long it takes, what a dead battery costs them, and what they
would pay for a five-minute swap. Their answers will change your design. 3 Fill in the sizing worksheet in §4.2. Compute both the off-grid and the solar-assisted grid-tied array, and state which you

recommend and why. 4 Compute the number of packs in circulation and price it. Notice that it dominates the capital cost. 5 Design the swap cabinet to the requirements in §4.4, keeping everything you build at 48 V and marking clearly on your
drawing which parts require a licensed contractor. 6 Fill in the cost model and compute payback with and without the PM E-DRIVE subsidy. Then write the one-page proposal
you would actually hand to your college administration.

modules.title: Project 2 — A Home Energy Audit Tool

intro.text: The cheapest kilowatt-hour is the one nobody uses. An energy audit routinely finds 10–20% of a household bill in places the occupant has never suspected — and the instrument that finds it costs under ₹3,000 and never touches a live conductor.

blocks.text:
Finding            Typical share of           Usual fix
                   bill
Standby / phantom 5–10%                       Set-top box, router, TV, microwave clock, chargers left plugged in. A switched power strip
load                                          recovers most of it for a few hundred rupees
An ageing          10–25% of the bill         A 12-year-old fridge can use two to three times a current 5-star model. Measure it over 24 h
refrigerator       on its own                 before assuming
Water heating 10–20% in winter A timer, a lower thermostat setting, or insulation on the tank and pipe run

Pumping            5–15% where there Usually a float switch that has failed, so the pump runs long after the tank is full. One of the
                   is an overhead tank highest-return fixes there is
Air conditioning   large and highly           Every degree of setpoint is worth several percent. Filter cleaning matters more than people
setpoint           variable                   believe

                                              on for two years
Note the ordering. Students almost always propose lighting first because it is visible; the money is usually in the fridge, the pump and standby.
The safety boundary for this project

You will not open the distribution board and you will not touch a live conductor. A split-core current transformer clips around the outside of an insulated cable and measures the magnetic field. That is the whole reason this project is appropriate for students.

One specific rule: never disconnect a current transformer from its burden while current is flowing in the cable it surrounds. An open-circuited CT develops a dangerously high voltage across its terminals. Use an SCT-013-030 type, which has the burden resistor built in and outputs a safe voltage directly — it removes the hazard by construction rather than by procedure.
Any clamping around a conductor inside a panel is done by a licensed electrician. Clamping around the flexible cord of a single appliance, outside any enclosure, is student work.

topics.title: Getting a real measurement, not a plausible one

blocks.text: // Sampling a 50 Hz waveform on an ESP32 to get REAL power. // The CT output is bipolar; the ADC is 0-3.3 V single-ended. So the signal // is DC-biased to mid-rail (1.65 V) with a divider and a coupling capacitor, // and we subtract that offset in software with a slow-tracking filter.
float offsetI = 2048, offsetV = 2048; // tracked, not assumed
void measure(float *Vrms, float *Irms, float *realP, float *pf) {
const int CYCLES = 20; // 20 cycles at 50 Hz = 400 ms
unsigned long t0 = millis();
double sumI2 = 0, sumV2 = 0, sumVI = 0;
long n = 0;
while (millis() - t0 < (CYCLES * 20)) { // whole cycles only, or the
int rawI = analogRead(PIN_I); // RMS figure wanders
int rawV = analogRead(PIN_V);
// slow high-pass: tracks the DC bias without following the signal offsetI += (rawI - offsetI) / 1024.0; offsetV += (rawV - offsetV) / 1024.0;
double i = rawI - offsetI; double v = rawV - offsetV;
sumI2 += i * i; // <-- this is what makes it sumV2 += v * v; sumVI += v * i; // REAL power, not apparent n++; }
*Irms = sqrt(sumI2 / n) * I_CAL_SCALE; *Vrms = sqrt(sumV2 / n) * V_CAL_SCALE; *realP = (sumVI / n) * I_CAL_SCALE * V_CAL_SCALE; *pf = (*Vrms * *Irms > 1.0) ? (*realP / (*Vrms * *Irms)) : 0.0; }

// Apparent power (Vrms x Irms) OVERSTATES what you are billed for on a // domestic meter, sometimes badly. A ceiling fan at low speed, an old // tube choke, a laptop charger or a fridge compressor can all sit at a // power factor of 0.5-0.7. Measuring current alone and multiplying by // 230 V would tell you the fan uses 90 W when it actually draws 55 W. // If you only measure current, report VA and SAY SO - do not call it watts.
Sampling for a whole number of cycles is not fussiness. A partial cycle biases the RMS calculation and your readings will drift for reasons you cannot find

• Calibrate current against a known load. A resistive heater or an incandescent bulb of known wattage has a power factor of essentially 1, so watts equal volts times amps. Adjust I_CAL_SCALE until your reading matches.

• Calibrate voltage against a multimeter, or against the utility meter if you can read it. • Cross-check the total against the electricity meter. Note the meter reading, run your instrument for 24 hours, and

compare. Agreement within about 10% is a good result for this hardware; beyond that, find the error before you present any savings figure. • If you cannot safely measure voltage, do not. Log current only, report in amperes and VA, and use a plug-in energy meter (available for a few hundred rupees) as your reference for appliance-level real power. An honest VA measurement is far better than a watts figure you cannot defend.
WORKSHEET — Home energy audit — run in this order

Collect 12 months of bills. Plot kWh by month. The shape tells you what is seasonal (cooling, water heating) before you measure anything. Note the tariff SLABS - the marginal unit may cost far more than the average, which changes every savings calculation.

DAY 1 THE STANDBY BASELINE (the single highest-value hour) At 2 a.m., or with everyone out, switch off everything the household believes is off. Measure the whole-house current. Whatever is left is your phantom load, running 8,760 hours a year. example: 45 W standby x 8,760 h = 394 kWh/yr = Rs 3,150 at Rs 8/kWh Then switch circuits off one at a time to locate it.

Clamp each major appliance in turn, or use a plug-in meter. Record: rated W | measured W | hours/day | duty cycle | kWh/day Refrigerator and AC MUST be measured over a full 24 hours - their duty cycle is the whole story and a spot reading tells you nothing.

Fridge interior temperature (should be 3-5 C; every degree colder costs) Fridge door seal: close it on a paper strip - if it pulls out easily, the seal is gone and the compressor is running to cool the kitchen Geyser thermostat setting and standing loss (measure overnight) Pump run time vs tank fill time - a failed float switch is common AC filter condition, setpoint, and whether doors are open

Rank findings by ANNUAL RUPEES SAVED, not by percentage and not by how interesting the engineering is. For each: cost to fix, saving per year, payback. Anything with a payback under a year gets done this month.
The standby baseline on Day 1 usually finds more money per hour invested than everything else combined, and it needs no permission and no rewiring.
Savings worksheet Measured kWh/yr ₹/yr saved Cost to fix Payback
Finding
Rank by the ₹/yr column. Present the top three, not all twelve — an audit report that lists everything gets ignored, and one that names three actions with rupee figures gets acted on.

DO THIS NOW — Audit a real household One week of measurement, one evening of analysis. 1 Build and calibrate the instrument. Do not proceed until it agrees with the utility meter within 10% over 24 hours. 2 Run the Day 1 standby baseline. Convert the result into rupees per year at the household’s marginal tariff and show them

that number — it is usually the moment the project becomes real to them. 3 Measure the refrigerator over a full 24 hours and compute its annual consumption. 4 Complete the savings worksheet and rank by rupees. 5 Implement the top finding, then measure again for a week to verify the saving actually appeared. A predicted saving is
a hypothesis; a measured one is a result. 6 Write the one-page report. Three actions, three rupee figures, three paybacks.

modules.title: Project 3 — A BMS for Second-Life Cells

intro.text: An EV battery retired at 70–80% of its original capacity still holds years of useful stationary life. Realising that value depends almost entirely on the battery management system — and on knowing which cells to refuse before you ever connect them.

The scope of this project, and why it is drawn here Build at a single module, at or below 60 V, and preferably below 30 V. A Nissan Leaf module is about 7.4 V; a Tesla module about 22 V; a 4S LFP pack is 12.8 V. Any of these teaches every concept in this chapter. Do not open, disassemble or reconfigure a complete EV traction pack. Those run at 350–800 V DC, they are lethal, and the interlocks and service-disconnect procedures that make them survivable are specialist training. Nothing in this chapter should be read as preparation for that work. Everything below — the protection thresholds, the balancing, the state-of-health test, the code — is identical in principle at 12 V and at 400 V. Learn it where a mistake costs a fuse.

blocks.text: Second-life cells arrive with an unknown history. Some of them should never be connected to anything. Inspect every module before it enters your workspace, and record the results.
CHECKLIST — Reject the module if any of these is true

□ Any swelling, bulging or deformation of a cell or pouch □ Any cell below about 2.0 V for LFP or 2.5 V for NMC — deep discharge causes internal copper plating and a □ Any sign of leakage, residue or crystallisation at a latent short terminal □ Cell-to-cell voltage spread greater than roughly 0.3 V at □ Any smell of solvent or sweetness — that is electrolyte rest □ Visible mechanical damage, dents, or crushed corners □ Terminal corrosion or damaged busbar threads □ Evidence of water or flood exposure (silt, corrosion, tide marks) □ No traceable origin — you cannot assess a history nobody can tell you
□ Any module from a vehicle known to have been in a fire or a serious collision
A rejected module is not rubbish to be thrown away — it is hazardous waste with a legal disposal route. See §7.6 on the Battery Waste Management Rules, and hand it to a registered recycler.

topics.title: What a BMS must actually do

blocks.text: Function What it means Consequence of omitting it
Measure Every cell voltage individually, pack current, Pack voltage alone hides a dying cell completely — one cell at 2.0 V
and at least two temperatures and one at 4.0 V looks identical to two at 3.0 V

Protect   Disconnect on over-voltage, under-voltage,          This is the function that prevents fires. It is not optional and it must act
          over-current, over-temperature and                  in hardware, not only in software
          under-temperature
Balance   Equalise cell states of charge, usually by          Without balancing, pack usable capacity falls to that of the weakest
          bleeding charge from the highest cells              cell and the spread widens every cycle
Estimate  State of charge and state of health                 You cannot manage what you cannot see; SoH is what tells you when
                                                              to retire a module
Report Log and communicate faults and trends A pack that fails silently teaches you nothing and warns you of nothing
SET THESE FROM YOUR CELL DATASHEET. The figures below are typical, not authoritative - a wrong threshold is how a good pack becomes a fire.

cell over-voltage cutoff    LFP (LiFePO4)           NMC / NCA
cell over-voltage recover   3.65 V                  4.20 V
cell under-voltage cutoff   3.40 V                  4.05 V
absolute floor (reject)     2.50 V                  3.00 V
balance start (top of chg)  2.00 V                  2.50 V
balance threshold (delta)   3.40 V                  4.00 V
charge temperature window   20 - 50 mV              20 - 50 mV
discharge temp window       0 to 45 C               0 to 45 C
nominal cell voltage        -20 to 60 C             -20 to 60 C
                            3.2 V                   3.6 - 3.7 V

Charging a lithium cell below freezing causes metallic lithium to plate on the anode. It is cumulative, it is invisible, and it eventually produces an internal short. In most of India this rarely matters - but it matters in the hills, and in an unheated room in a north Indian January. Interlock it: no charge below 0 C, no exceptions.

DEFENCE IN DEPTH - three layers, and you need all three 1. SOFTWARE the MCU opens the contactor on a fault 2. HARDWARE the analogue front-end asserts a protection output independently of the MCU, so a hung MCU is not fatal 3. PASSIVE a correctly sized fuse in the pack, and a thermal fuse. It does not need firmware and cannot be argued with.
Layer 3 is what saves you when layers 1 and 2 both have bugs, which on a first student BMS they will
│ MODULE (e.g. 4S LFP, 12.8 V nominal) │
│ │ │ │ sense taps └───▶│ CONTACTOR│
▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ (fused, 100 R) │ or MOSFET│
│ - per-cell ADC │ independent hardware protect
│ - passive balancing FETs │
│ - over/under voltage comparators │ ┌──────────────────────┐
│ - coulomb counter │◀──I2C──│ MCU (ESP32) │
▲ │ - balancing policy │
│ thermistors │ - logging, telemetry │
┌─────┴──────┐ │ - software protect │

Use an AFE chip rather than measuring cells with the MCU's ADC. Cell sensing is a common-mode problem: cell 4's terminals sit 9.6 V above ground, and a naive divider-per-cell arrangement is inaccurate, temperature-dependent, and drains cells unevenly - which creates the very imbalance you are trying to fix.
Figure 6.1 — Always fuse the sense wires. A shorted sense lead becomes a direct path across several cells, and it is the most common way a home-built BMS starts a fire.

• Passive balancing bleeds the highest cells through a resistor as heat. Simple, cheap, built into most AFE chips, and slow — typically 50–200 mA. It is what you should build. Balance only near the top of charge, where cell voltages actually separate.
• Active balancing moves charge from strong cells to weak ones. Far more efficient and considerably more complex. Not a first project.

• State of charge by voltage alone fails on LFP. The LFP discharge curve is almost flat between roughly 20% and 80% — a swing of a few tens of millivolts covers most of the usable range, so open-circuit voltage cannot resolve it. NMC has a steeper curve and is more forgiving.

• So use coulomb counting, corrected at the ends. Integrate current in and out to track charge, and re-zero the estimate whenever the pack reaches a known point — full charge, or a rest at a voltage on the steep part of the curve. Coulomb counting drifts; the end-point corrections are what stop the drift accumulating.
• State of health is capacity, measured. Not guessed from voltage, not inferred from age. See the test below.
WORKSHEET — Capacity and state-of-health test — the number that matters
EQUIPMENT adjustable DC load or a known resistive load, a coulomb counter or shunt + ADC, thermocouple, metal container, sand bucket, fire blanket, ventilation, second person present
1. Bring the module to full charge at low current (0.2C or less) with balancing enabled. Let it rest 2 hours. Record every cell voltage.
2. Discharge at a constant, modest rate (0.2C) to the under-voltage cutoff of the FIRST cell to reach it - not to a pack-level voltage. The weakest cell defines the module. Log Ah continuously.
3. Measured capacity = the Ah delivered. SoH = measured capacity / original rated capacity
example: a Leaf module rated 60 Ah delivers 44 Ah SoH = 44 / 60 = 73% -> viable for stationary use
4. Rest 2 hours. Record every cell voltage again. Compute the spread.
spread < 30 mV healthy, balanced
30 - 100 mV needs balancing; usable
> 100 mV after balancing -> one cell is failing. RETIRE the module.
5. Repeat at a higher rate (0.5C) and compare. A large capacity drop with rate indicates high internal resistance, which is the other ageing mechanism and the one that causes heating under load.
SoH > 80% good stationary second life
70 - 80% usable, derate the expected capacity accordingly
< 70% marginal; only worth it if the module was free
any cell that will not hold balance -> the module is done. Recycle it.
Do this test on every incoming module and keep the records. The measured capacity, not the label, is what you design your system around.
// BMS main loop. Software layer only - the AFE hardware protection and // the pack fuse (6.3) sit underneath this and do not depend on it.
#define NCELLS 4 float vcell[NCELLS], packI, tempC[2];
typedef enum { IDLE, CHARGING, DISCHARGING, PROTECT, FAULT_LATCH } BmsState; BmsState state = IDLE; uint32_t protectEnteredMs = 0;
void bmsLoop(float dt) { afeReadCells(vcell, NCELLS); packI = afeReadCurrent(); afeReadTemps(tempC, 2);
float vmax = maxOf(vcell, NCELLS), vmin = minOf(vcell, NCELLS); float spread = vmax - vmin; float tmax = fmaxf(tempC[0], tempC[1]);
// ---- coulomb counting, corrected at the ends
coulombs += packI * dt; // signed: + charge, - load
if (vmax >= V_FULL && fabsf(packI) < I_REST) coulombs = capacityAs;
if (vmin <= V_EMPTY) coulombs = 0;
soc = 100.0f * coulombs / capacityAs;
// ---- protection, evaluated EVERY cycle regardless of state
uint16_t f = 0;
if (vmax > V_CELL_OV) f |= F_OVERVOLT;
if (vmin < V_CELL_UV) f |= F_UNDERVOLT;
if (fabsf(packI) > I_MAX) f |= F_OVERCURRENT;
if (tmax > T_MAX) f |= F_OVERTEMP;
if (packI > 0 && tempC[0] < T_CHARGE_MIN) f |= F_COLD_CHARGE; // see 6.3
if (spread > SPREAD_FAULT) f |= F_IMBALANCE;
if (f) {
openContactor(); // act first, log second
logFault(f, vcell, packI, tempC);
state = (f & (F_OVERTEMP | F_COLD_CHARGE)) ? FAULT_LATCH : PROTECT;
protectEnteredMs = millis();
return; // do nothing else this cycle
// ---- recovery: hysteresis AND a dwell time, never an instant retry
if (state == PROTECT) {
bool clear = (vmax < V_CELL_OV_RECOVER) && (vmin > V_CELL_UV_RECOVER)
&& (tmax < T_MAX - 5.0f);
if (clear && (millis() - protectEnteredMs > RECOVER_DWELL_MS)) {
closeContactor(); state = IDLE;
return;
if (state == FAULT_LATCH) return; // needs a human. By design.
// ---- passive balancing: only near top of charge, only one cell at a time if (vmax > V_BALANCE_START && spread > SPREAD_BALANCE)
afeEnableBalance(indexOfMax(vcell, NCELLS)); else
afeDisableBalance();
state = (packI > I_REST) ? CHARGING : (packI < -I_REST) ? DISCHARGING : IDLE;

// Two design decisions worth arguing about, and here is the argument: // - Thermal faults LATCH. A pack that overheated once will overheat // again, and an automatic retry loop on a warm pack is exactly how a // recoverable fault becomes a fire. // - Recovery needs hysteresis AND dwell. Without both, a pack sitting // at the threshold chatters the contactor thousands of times an hour // and welds it closed - after which you have no protection at all.
DO THIS NOW — Build and prove the BMS
Three weekends. Every step happens with a supervisor and the fire kit present.
1 Source one low-voltage module (4S LFP, or a single Leaf or Tesla module). Run the incoming inspection checklist and record every observation with photographs.
2 Build the sense harness with a fuse in every sense lead. Check every connection twice for polarity before powering anything.
3 Bring up the AFE and read all cell voltages. Verify each against a multimeter before you trust a single reading from the chip.

4 Implement protections in software, then test each one deliberately — trigger over-voltage with a bench supply, trigger over-temperature with a hair dryer, trigger over-current with a known load. An untested protection is not a protection.

5 Run the capacity test and compute SoH. Compare against the module’s original rating. 6 Enable balancing and run three full cycles. Plot the cell spread at the top of each charge. A falling spread means it is
working; a spread that will not close means you have found a bad cell, which is itself a successful result.

intro.text: Policy is not paperwork bolted on at the end. It routinely changes which design wins — a subsidy can halve a payback period, and a metering rule can decide whether an extra kilowatt of array is worth installing at all. Read this before you finalise a design, not after.

How to use this chapter Everything here was verified in mid-2026. Schemes are amended, extended, exhausted and replaced — and several below carry explicit terminal dates that fall within the next two years. Use this chapter to learn the structure: who administers what, what the eligibility hinges on, and where the money actually comes from. Then confirm every number on the official portal on the day you apply.

topics.title: PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana — residential rooftop solar

blocks.text:

What it is

Free units         ₹30,000 per kW for the first 2 kW, plus ₹18,000 for the third kW. So ₹30,000 at 1 kW, ₹60,000 at 2 kW, and ₹78,000

pmsuryaghar.gov.in
Why roughly one application in three is rejected

The common causes are administrative rather than technical: the electricity bill is in a parent’s or spouse’s name but the Aadhaar used is the applicant’s; the sanctioned load or connection category does not match; documents are illegible; the chosen vendor is not empanelled; or the installed module model is not actually on the ALMM list even though the brand is. Check the specific model number against the list before installation, not after.

topics.title: Net metering — and why the variant matters more than the rate

blocks.text: Metering policy is set by each state’s electricity regulatory commission, so the rules genuinely differ across the country. What does not differ is the structure. There are three arrangements, and which one you get changes the economics of your design substantially:

Arrangement          How it works                                      Effect on your design
Net metering
                     Exported units are netted against imported        The best case for the consumer. Oversizing slightly is rational, because
Net billing / net    units. You are billed on the net. In effect,      surplus carries full retail value
feed-in              export is credited at the retail tariff
                                                                       Self-consumption becomes much more valuable than export. Size
Gross metering       Import is billed at the retail tariff; export is  closer to the daytime load, and consider shifting loads into daylight
                     credited at a separate, usually lower, rate       hours
                     All generation is sold to the DISCOM at a fixed   The system becomes a small generation business rather than a
                     tariff; all consumption is bought at retail       bill-offset. The economics depend entirely on the feed-in rate

• Check the capacity cap. Most states limit net metering for residential consumers, commonly at around 10 kW, and often also cap total rooftop solar as a percentage of the distribution transformer capacity — which means your neighbour installing first can consume the available headroom.
• Check the settlement period. Monthly, half-yearly or annual settlement changes how much of your seasonal surplus survives to be used.
• Check what happens to unused credit at the end of the settlement period. Some states pay for it at a low rate; some simply lapse it.
• Get the technical feasibility approval before you buy anything. The DISCOM must confirm the connection can accept your system. Projects have been bought and then refused connection.

topics.title: ALMM — the list that decides whether you qualify

blocks.text: The Approved List of Models and Manufacturers is maintained by MNRE. List-I covers solar modules and List-II covers solar cells. For government-supported projects — which includes PM Surya Ghar — equipment must be ALMM-listed. Two practical consequences: the module model number must appear on the list, not merely the manufacturer’s name; and listings are added and removed over time, so verify on the current published list rather than on a vendor’s assurance or an old PDF.

The line that matters for Chapter 4

If your college station is publicly accessible, the charging equipment and the upstream electrical work may be substantially or fully funded. That transforms the payback calculation in §4.5 — and it is exactly the kind of provision that student teams never check because it sounds like something only companies can access. Confirm current eligibility and the application route with your state nodal agency before you assume either way.

topics.title: State schemes and other central programmes

blocks.text: • State EV and solar policies stack on top of central ones, and they vary widely. As illustrative examples from 2026: Gujarat has offered capital subsidy on public EV charging installations along with electricity duty exemption and reduced road tax; Tamil Nadu has offered road tax waivers and land cost support; Punjab has offered charging station subsidies and purchase incentives for e-two-wheelers and e-autos; Rajasthan adds a state top-up on the PM Surya Ghar subsidy. Check your own state’s current policy — these change and several carry expiry dates.

• PM-KUSUM supports solar in agriculture: standalone solar pumps, solarisation of existing grid-connected pumps, and small solar plants on farmers’ land. If your project touches irrigation, this is the relevant scheme rather than PM Surya Ghar.

• Electricity duty and road tax exemptions are often where the quiet money is for a charging business — an exemption on duty applies every month for years, and compounds far beyond a one-time capital subsidy.
• Discom empanelment. For rooftop solar, only vendors empanelled with your DISCOM can execute a subsidised installation. Check the list before selecting a vendor, not after.

topics.title: Battery waste — a legal obligation, not an afterthought

blocks.text: The Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 place Extended Producer Responsibility on producers of all battery types, require registration and reporting on the CPCB portal, set recycling and recovery targets, and prohibit disposal of batteries in landfill or by incineration. For a student project the practical implications are direct and short: every cell you reject in §6.1, and every pack you eventually retire, must go to a registered recycler and not into a bin. Record where each one went. If your project ever becomes a product, the EPR obligations become yours, and designing for disassembly and recovery from the start is far cheaper than retrofitting it.

Sources and dates. PM Surya Ghar figures — ₹30,000/kW to 2 kW, ₹18,000 for the third kW, ₹78,000 cap, ALMM requirement, roughly 40 lakh households by mid-2026 — are as published by MNRE and reported to Parliament in 2026. PM E-DRIVE details — the ₹10,900 crore outlay, the August 2025 extension to four years within the same outlay, the terminal dates of 31 July 2026 for e-2W and 31 March 2028 for e-rickshaws and e-carts, and the charging infrastructure guidelines including up to 100% support for educational institutions offering free public access — are as notified by the Ministry of Heavy Industries. Metering rules are set by state commissions and are not summarised here for that reason. Every one of these can change with a notification; verify before you rely on it.

And the sentence this guide is built around. The best energy system is the one that is still running, safely, in year seven — not the one with the highest efficiency on a datasheet. That means designing for dust rather than for laboratory irradiance, for the worst monsoon month rather than the annual average, for the battery you can actually afford to replace, and for the person who will have to clean it. Deployable beats ideal, every time, and safety comes before both.
